title: Warp Drive Feasibility
problem: Could a spacetime geometry that resembles a warp drive ever become an engineering system? Assess proposed concepts against physical realizability and testable engineering requirements. Distinguish mathematical spacetime metrics from physically realizable propulsion systems. Review the assumptions about stress-energy, energy density, stability, causality, control, materials, and navigation; trace claims to primary sources; and test quantitative estimates for dimensional and physical consistency. Identify which obstacles are established by current theory or evidence, which depend on unresolved physics, and what experiment or calculation could reduce the uncertainty. Set aside the assumption that a warp drive must violate the speed-of-light limit: assess how proposed spacetime geometries distinguish local motion from effective travel over distance. Do not treat a proposed metric by itself as a complete engineering design.

strategies.title: Translate concept into constraints
strategies.approach: Choose one proposed metric or propulsion concept and make a requirements table for energy, stress-energy, stability, control, and causality. Mark each entry as established physics, a model-dependent calculation, or an unverified assumption; do not turn a conceptual requirement into an available engineering capability.

strategies.title: Look for a decisive failure test
strategies.approach: Pick one obstacle such as energy conditions, horizon control, or backreaction. State a calculation or observation that could rule out the chosen concept under explicit assumptions, then compare it with a fundamentally different route.
strategies.summary: Look for a decisive failure test
